content: Sirenia is an order of fully aquatic mammals that are herbivorous in nature. These animals inhabit a variety of aquatic environments, including rivers, estuaries, coastal marine waters, swamps, and marine wetlands. The evolutionary history of this order dates back to the Eocene epoch, over 50 million years ago. Members of this order, such as manatees and the dugong, exhibit significant adaptations to their aquatic lifestyle. Their forelimbs have evolved into flipper-like structures used for steering, while their tails have transformed into paddle-like appendages that provide propulsion. The hind limbs are reduced to small vestigial bones embedded deep within the musculature. Although they appear to have a fat body composition, their bodies are actually fusiform, hydrodynamic, and highly muscular, which aids in efficient movement through water. Their skulls are uniquely adapted to facilitate breathing at the water's surface, and their dentition is significantly reduced. The skeletal structure of both manatees and dugongs is characterized by extremely dense bones, which counteract the buoyancy provided by their blubber. Manatees, in particular, possess a remarkable ability to continuously produce new teeth as their anterior teeth wear down. Sirenians have only two mammary glands, located beneath their forelimbs, a feature they share with their closest living relatives, the elephants. The order Sirenia includes three species of manatees (family Trichechidae) and the dugong (family Dugongidae), all of which are classified as endangered species. These animals face significant threats to their survival due to habitat loss and the adverse effects of human population growth and coastal development. One species, the Steller's sea cow, has already been driven to extinction by human hunting. Manatees and dugongs are the only marine mammals that are strictly herbivorous. Unlike other marine mammals such as dolphins, whales, seals, sea lions, sea otters, and walruses, sirenians primarily consume seagrasses and other aquatic vegetation. They have an exceptionally low metabolic rate and are poorly adapted to tolerate cold water. Although rare instances of sirenians consuming dead animals, such as seagulls, have been observed, their diet is predominantly plant-based. Similar to dolphins and whales, manatees and dugongs are fully aquatic and never leave the water, even for birthing. Occasionally, they have been observed feeding on grass clippings from residential areas near waterways, but only the upper portion of their bodies emerges from the water during such events. Due to their dietary and physiological requirements, sirenians are restricted to warm, shallow coastal waters, estuaries, and rivers that support healthy ecosystems with abundant seagrass and vegetation. The family Trichechidae (manatees) differs from the family Dugongidae (dugongs) in several anatomical features, including the shape of the skull and tail. The taxonomy of the order Sirenia includes both extant and extinct genera and species. Some notable extinct genera include †Ishatherium, †Pezosiren, †Prorastomus, and †Protosiren. The family Dugongidae includes the extant Dugong (Dugong dugon) and extinct genera such as †Sirenotherium, †Dusisiren, and †Hydrodamalis, the latter of which includes the extinct Steller's sea cow (†Hydrodamalis gigas). The family Trichechidae includes the following species of manatees: West Indian Manatee (Trichechus manatus), which is further divided into subspecies: Antillean Manatee (Trichechus manatus manatus) Florida Manatee (Trichechus manatus latirostris) African Manatee (Trichechus senegalensis) Amazonian Manatee (Trichechus inunguis) Dwarf Manatee (Trichechus bernhardi), though the validity of this species is questionable. Extinct species within the order Sirenia are denoted with the symbol †.
